```{r, include = FALSE}
# the full examples run when the package is built; CRAN checks skip them for time
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true"), collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(bayescompR)
```

Gradient based inference needs the gradient of the log density with
respect to the unconstrained parameters. bayescompR computes it with
reverse mode automatic differentiation written in R, and maps between
constrained and unconstrained parameters with Stan's transforms. This
vignette explains both and shows how to check them.

## The log density

For parameters $\theta$ with constraints, bayescompR works with
unconstrained values $u$ and $\theta = T(u)$. The density sampled is

$$\log p(u) = \text{target}(T(u)) + \log \left| \det J_T(u) \right|,$$

where `target` is accumulated by the model block. With
`jacobian = FALSE` the second term is dropped (maximum likelihood style
optimization); with `propto = TRUE` constant terms of `~` statements are
dropped, as during sampling.

```{r}
m <- bayescomp_model("
parameters { real<lower=0> sigma; }
model { sigma ~ exponential(2); }")
u <- log(0.7)
c(full = bayescomp_log_prob(m, u),
  by_hand = dexp(0.7, 2, log = TRUE) + u,
  no_jacobian = bayescomp_log_prob(m, u, jacobian = FALSE))
```

## Reverse mode AD

During a gradient evaluation every operation on a parameter dependent value
creates a node on a tape recording its inputs and local partial
derivatives. The backward pass visits the nodes in reverse order and
accumulates adjoints, so the cost of the full gradient is a small multiple
of the cost of the log density, whatever the number of parameters.

Values on the tape have class `bcad`. Operations are vectorized: a node
holds a whole vector or matrix, not a scalar, so `y ~ normal(mu, sigma)`
over a vector of a million elements is one node. Densities and most
library functions are fused: a single node with analytic partial
derivatives rather than a chain of elementary operations, which keeps the
tape short in the R interpreter. Linear algebra uses matrix adjoint rules,
for example $\bar A = -A^{-T} \bar C A^{-T}$ for $C = A^{-1}$ and the
Cholesky adjoint of Murray (2016).

`bayescomp_grad_log_prob()` returns the gradient; comparing it with finite
differences is the basic check of any implementation:

```{r}
m <- bayescomp_model("
data { int N; vector[N] y; matrix[N, 2] X; }
parameters { vector[2] beta; real<lower=0> sigma; cholesky_factor_corr[2] L; }
model {
  beta ~ multi_normal_cholesky(rep_vector(0, 2), diag_pre_multiply([1, 2]', L));
  sigma ~ student_t(3, 0, 1);
  L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  y ~ normal(X * beta, sigma);
}", data = list(N = 4, y = c(1, 2, 0.5, 3), X = cbind(1, 1:4)))
u <- c(0.2, -0.1, 0.3, 0.4)
g <- bayescomp_grad_log_prob(m, u)
fd <- vapply(seq_along(u), function(i) {
  e <- replace(numeric(4), i, 1e-6)
  (bayescomp_log_prob(m, u + e) - bayescomp_log_prob(m, u - e)) / 2e-6
}, 0)
rbind(ad = as.vector(g), finite_difference = fd)
max(abs(g - fd))
```

The test suite runs this comparison for every elementwise function, every
distribution and the linear algebra functions.

## Transforms

Each constrained type uses the transform of the Stan Reference Manual
(version 2.40, "Constraint Transforms"), with the same log Jacobian, so
`lp__` values agree with Stan's.

| Type | Unconstrained size | Transform |
|------|-------------------|-----------|
| `real<lower=a>` | 1 | $a + e^u$ |
| `real<upper=b>` | 1 | $b - e^u$ |
| `real<lower=a, upper=b>` | 1 | $a + (b - a)\,\text{logit}^{-1}(u)$ |
| `real<offset=m, multiplier=s>` | 1 | $m + s u$ |
| `ordered[K]` | K | $x_1 = u_1$, $x_k = x_{k-1} + e^{u_k}$ |
| `positive_ordered[K]` | K | as ordered with $x_1 = e^{u_1}$ |
| `simplex[K]` | K - 1 | softmax of the isometric sum to zero vector |
| `sum_to_zero_vector[K]` | K - 1 | orthonormal basis of the sum to zero subspace |
| `sum_to_zero_matrix[N, M]` | (N - 1)(M - 1) | the vector transform on both margins |
| `unit_vector[K]` | K | $u / \lVert u \rVert$ with a standard normal term on $\lVert u \rVert$ |
| `cholesky_factor_corr[K]` | K(K - 1)/2 | canonical partial correlations via `tanh` |
| `corr_matrix[K]` | K(K - 1)/2 | $L L^T$ with the Lewandowski, Kurowicka and Joe Jacobian |
| `cholesky_factor_cov[M, N]` | N(N + 1)/2 + (M - N)N | lower triangle with log diagonal |
| `cov_matrix[K]` | K(K + 1)/2 | $L L^T$ with log diagonal of $L$ |
| `column_stochastic_matrix[N, M]` | (N - 1)M | simplex transform on each column |
| `row_stochastic_matrix[N, M]` | N(M - 1) | simplex transform on each row |

Arrays of constrained types transform each element. Unconstrained values
are ordered as in Stan: array elements in row major order, the elements of
each vector or matrix in column major order.

```{r}
m <- bayescomp_model("parameters { simplex[3] theta; cov_matrix[2] S; } model { }")
p <- bayescomp_constrain(m, c(0.3, -0.2, 0.1, 0.5, 0.2))
p
bayescomp_unconstrain(m, p)
```

Constraints are checked when values are read: data and initial values that
violate them are rejected, and transformed parameters are validated after
every evaluation.

```{r, error = TRUE}
bayescomp_unconstrain(m, list(theta = c(0.5, 0.6, -0.1), S = diag(2)))
```

## Checking a Jacobian

The log Jacobian is the log absolute determinant of the derivative of the
transform with respect to the free coordinates. For an ordered vector:

```{r}
m <- bayescomp_model("parameters { ordered[3] x; } model { }")
u <- c(0.4, -0.3, 0.8)
f <- function(u) bayescomp_constrain(m, u)$x
J <- vapply(1:3, function(i) {
  e <- replace(numeric(3), i, 1e-6)
  (f(u + e) - f(u - e)) / 2e-6
}, numeric(3))
c(numeric = log(abs(det(J))), bayescompR = bayescomp_log_prob(m, u))
```
